content: Chest X-ray (CXR) and the WHO-recommended four-symptom screen (W4SS) are used in parallel to exclude active tuberculosis (TB) disease before initiating TB preventive treatment (TPT) in people living with HIV who are on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Evidence from eight studies conducted in various countries, including Benin, Botswana, Brazil, Guinea, India, Kenya, Malawi, Myanmar, Peru, South Africa, and Zimbabwe, involving 6,238 participants, was reviewed to inform the 2021 TB screening guidelines. CXR alone demonstrated similar sensitivity and either similar or higher specificity compared to the W4SS across all subpopulations. When CXR was performed after a positive W4SS, its sensitivity was either lower or similar, while its specificity was either higher or similar. When CXR and W4SS were used in parallel, sensitivity was higher or similar, and specificity remained similar. Recommendation 12 pertains to the use of C-reactive protein (CRP) for screening adults and adolescents with HIV for TB disease. CRP, a marker of general inflammation, can be measured using point-of-care tests with capillary blood obtained via finger prick. Evidence from six studies conducted in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda, involving 3,971 participants, was reviewed. The diagnostic accuracy of CRP was assessed using cut-off values of >5 mg/L and >10 mg/L as indicators of TB disease. The accuracy of CRP at these thresholds was found to be similar or superior to that of the W4SS. A cut-off value of >5 mg/L was recommended due to its lower threshold for abnormality in clinical settings and its higher sensitivity compared to >10 mg/L. Meta-analysis of individual patient data using a CRP cut-off of >5 mg/L showed similar sensitivity and higher or similar specificity compared to the W4SS across all subpopulations. When CRP was combined with the W4SS and used in parallel, it demonstrated similar or greater sensitivity and specificity than the W4SS alone, depending on the cut-off threshold and subpopulation assessed. CRP was most accurate for outpatients not on ART, with a sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 37% in this subpopulation. When performed sequentially after a positive W4SS in people with HIV not on ART, CRP with a cut-off of >5 mg/L had similar sensitivity (84%) but significantly higher specificity (64%) compared to the W4SS alone. However, the specificity of CRP for TB screening in inpatients with HIV was extremely low, likely due to competing comorbidities that also elevate CRP levels and cause similar symptoms. Recommendation 13 addresses the use of molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) for screening adults and adolescents with HIV for TB disease. A systematic review of 14 studies involving 9,209 participants evaluated the performance of mWRDs, with the Xpert MTB/RIF assay being the most commonly used. The sensitivity of mWRDs alone was 69%, with a specificity of 98%. When the W4SS was followed by an mWRD, sensitivity was 62%, and specificity was 99%. The accuracy of mWRDs was not significantly different from that of the W4SS followed by mWRDs across various subpopulations. For children under 5 years of age who are close contacts of a person with TB, symptom-based screening (including cough, fever, or poor weight gain) has been shown to be a safe and feasible strategy, even in resource-limited settings. Evidence from four studies involving 2,695 participants indicated a pooled sensitivity of 89% and specificity of 69% for symptom screening. For children and adolescents under 15 years of age exposed to TB, CXR screening for abnormalities suggestive of TB had a pooled sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 91%. For HIV-negative household contacts aged 5 years or older and other risk groups, the absence of TB symptoms and abnormal CXR findings can be used to rule out TB disease before initiating TPT. This recommendation is conditional due to very low certainty of evidence. A systematic review determined the sensitivity and specificity of symptom-based screening and/or CXR for ruling out TB disease in HIV-negative individuals and those with unknown HIV status. The combination of any TB symptoms and any abnormal CXR findings had the highest sensitivity (100%) and negative predictive value (100%) for ruling out TB. In a hypothetical population with a TB prevalence of 2%, using symptom screening alone would misclassify 54 people with TB as not having the disease, while using CXR abnormalities alone would misclassify 12 people. Combining symptom screening with CXR abnormalities would result in no misclassification of TB cases. Recommendations 15 and 16 relate to the use of symptom screening, CXR, or mWRDs, alone or in combination, for screening adults and adolescents for TB disease. A systematic review of diagnostic accuracy for symptom screening and CXR in individuals aged 15 years or older with negative or unknown HIV status showed that CXR is highly sensitive and specific, while mWRDs are less sensitive for screening but highly specific. Symptom screening is accessible and can be repeated as needed, but additional resources are required for CXR and mWRDs. The WHO guidelines emphasize that national programs should specify the necessary investigations to rule out TB disease. However, the absence of these investigations should not be a barrier to initiating TPT, particularly for household contacts under 5 years of age. Symptom screening with or without CXR is considered acceptable for individuals and program managers. CXR can increase healthcare providers' confidence in ruling out TB disease and reduce concerns about inappropriate TPT administration. The use of computer-aided detection (CAD) with digital CXR is conditionally recommended for TB screening and triage in individuals aged 15 years or older. In conclusion, a parallel screening algorithm combining any TB symptoms and any abnormal CXR findings is highly sensitive. The absence of TB symptoms and abnormal CXR findings can be used to exclude pulmonary TB disease before initiating TPT in HIV-negative household contacts aged 5 years or older and other risk groups. mWRDs may be useful when higher specificity is required, such as in settings with limited capacity for confirmatory testing.
